newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia's NatMut says float demand strong.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia's NatMut says float demand strong.

text.p: Australian life office National Mutual Holdings Ltd said on Wednesday it continued to meet with strong demand for its stock in its current share market offering.

"The retail offering is going to expectations in Australia...Institutional demand is very strong," managing director National Mutual Life Tony Killen told reporters at the launch of the company's Internet World Wide Web site.

National Mutual, which plans to list on the Australian and New Zealand exchanges next month has said more than half of its 1.2 billion policy-holders had elected to take up their entitlement to shares in the float.
Killen said a large proportion of the retail demand was coming from existing policy-holders who wanted to top up their entitlements.

National Mutual has set an offer price of A$1.50 per share for retail investors and indicated a price range of between A$1.35 and A$1.55 for institutional investors, who will bid for at least 60 percent of the shares on public sale.
The retail price of A$1.50 a share translated to a market capitalisation of about A$2.5 billion.
Killen also said National Mutual's efforts to obtain license to operate in China had not been hobbled by a decision by Prime Minister John Howard to meet with exiled spiritual leader the Dalai Lama.
"It hasn't affected out plans. We hope that it won't over the short to medium term," he said.

Beijing, which regards the Buddhist god-king as a pro-independence campaigner bent on splitting China, threatened trade retaliation on Tuesday after Howard announced he would meet the Dalai Lama on Thursday.
Deputy prime minister Tim Fischer said earlier on Wednesday he did not expect the meeting to upset ties with China.
Killen said Chinese officials had not contacted National Mutual's Chinese representatives since the meeting announcement and the insurer would not be seeking talks with the Australian government.
"This is a political issue which we really don't get involved in," he said.
